Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Opinion AI or Be Left Behind: Ghana’s opportunity to leapfrog into the intelligent economy Source : Eugene O. Aryeetey 5 November 2026 2:20pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Artificial intelligence could strengthen Ghana’s classrooms, businesses, farms and public institutions. Lasting gains will depend on the skills we build, the problems we solve, and how much value stays in the country.
Ghana could spend heavily on artificial intelligence and still miss its biggest economic opportunity. Buying software, announcing computing centres and handing out training certificates will achieve little if people cannot use the technology to do better work or build viable businesses.
The more important question is who will develop, adapt, maintain and earn from the systems entering our economy. Ghana must become more than a customer for intelligence developed elsewhere. We need the capacity to apply it to our own problems and retain a meaningful share of the value it creates.
That ambition now has a policy foundation. Ghana formally launched its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy on 24 April 2026. The government has also announced an AI computing centre and, in October, a centralised technical review mechanism for public-sector AI acquisitions. These are significant commitments. Their announcement alone does not establish that infrastructure is operational or that services have improved.
The next phase deserves a more demanding public conversation: what will change for the teacher preparing lessons, the graduate seeking work, the trader managing stock and the farmer deciding when to plant?
The technology need not be mysterious. Generative AI produces material such as text, images and software code. Large language models power many conversational tools. AI agents can go further by using authorised software tools to carry out parts of a task. These capabilities overlap, and none makes a system automatically accurate or trustworthy.
In education, an assistant could help a teacher prepare practice exercises for learners at different levels. A student could ask for another explanation of a difficult concept. But a convincing wrong answer is still wrong, and a completed AI-generated assignment does not demonstrate understanding.
Teachers therefore need practical training, time to evaluate tools and control over classroom use. Schools need reliable electricity, affordable connectivity and suitable devices. Introducing advanced tools where those basics are missing risks widening the gap between well-resourced schools and everyone else.
Ghanaian-language resources should be part of this effort. Universities, teachers and language specialists could help build and test tools that reflect how people actually speak and learn. Translation alone will not guarantee accuracy. Assessments should reward reasoning and the ability to explain an answer, while protecting children’s personal information.
The same emphasis on real competence should guide workforce policy. The Ghana Statistical Service reported that unemployment among people aged 15 to 35 averaged 21.9 per cent during the first three quarters of 2025. That is a labour-market challenge, not a measure of jobs lost to AI. It does, however, underline why promises about future employment deserve scrutiny.
Training should connect to actual work: checking accounts, managing records, writing software, supporting customers or interpreting technical information. Success means demonstrable skills, useful placements and better earnings or productivity. Registration totals and certificates cannot tell us whether those outcomes have occurred.
Employers should involve workers when redesigning jobs and provide credible routes into new roles where tasks are displaced. Ghana should prepare people to exercise judgment alongside AI, rather than assume that learning to prompt a chatbot is an employment strategy.
For a small enterprise, the most valuable AI application may be an unglamorous one. Better stock records, quicker quotations or fewer invoicing mistakes could matter more than an impressive demonstration.
Consider a distributor using an assistant to summarise sales, flag possible shortages and prepare a draft purchase order. This is a proposed use, not a claim about a verified Ghanaian deployment. Test its value against the existing workflow: does it save staff time, reduce errors, and justify its full cost? Spending decisions should remain subject to clear approval limits.
Ghanaian technology firms could build businesses around these needs through integration, local-language services, secure automation, and ongoing support. Universities could contribute research and testing. Public procurement could create opportunities for capable local suppliers, provided contracts reward performance and genuine knowledge transfer rather than local branding alone.
Imported models and cloud services can be useful components. Domestic capability does not require Ghana to reproduce every technology. It requires enough expertise and bargaining power to choose suppliers, protect data, maintain systems and change providers when necessary.
The announced public-sector review mechanism recognises interoperability, cybersecurity and local skills transfer. The practical test will be the contracts and delivery: who can repair a system, who controls its data, and what happens when a vendor raises prices or leaves?
Agriculture offers a particularly clear test of whether AI can serve everyday needs. An extension officer could use a validated tool to help explain crop advice or interpret field information. Voice-based services could make useful information accessible to farmers who are less comfortable with written digital tools.
Local activity already exists to learn from. Farmerline reported in 2025 that its Mergdata and Darli-enabled services distributed multilingual audio content to farmers in northern Ghana. That is evidence of a provider-reported service in use, not independent proof that AI raised yields or incomes.
The distinction matters. Advice about planting, pests or fertiliser must fit local conditions and be checked by qualified agricultural specialists. Incorrect recommendations can cost a farmer an entire season. Digital advice also cannot supply missing irrigation, repair a road or guarantee a buyer.
Agricultural pilots should therefore work with extension services and farmer organisations, measuring advice quality, crop losses, costs and farm income. Tools that cannot demonstrate practical benefit should be changed or dropped. Food security requires stronger farming systems, with AI supporting them where it proves useful.
The national-security case also needs discipline. A practical starting point is cybersecurity: protecting public records, communications, payments and other essential systems. AI could help analysts organise incident reports and identify suspicious patterns, but having an AI tool does not guarantee better protection.
Ghana has an existing Cyber Security Authority and national incident-response capacity. New investments should strengthen those institutions rather than assume the country is starting from nothing. Controlled trials should measure missed threats, false alarms and response times before systems receive wider authority.
Greater autonomy creates additional risk. An assistant that summarises a report has different powers from an agent allowed to move money, alter records or operate infrastructure. Limit access to what each task requires. High-impact actions should need human approval, with protected records of what happened and a way to stop the system.
National security must not become a blanket justification for intrusive surveillance or decisions citizens cannot challenge. Privacy, accountability, and effective oversight should be built into deployments from the start.
The World Bank’s 2025 Digital Progress and Trends Report identifies four foundations for AI development: connectivity, computing resources, relevant data and skills. These are a useful reminder that an intelligent economy depends on much more than software. Ghana also needs public trust, earned through reliable performance and meaningful accountability.
That calls for a practical delivery agenda. The ministry responsible for digital technology and sector agencies should publish clear responsibilities, funding status and results for priority projects. Announced investment, released funds, completed infrastructure and demonstrated public benefit should appear as separate milestones.
Before scaling a pilot, its owner should show what improved against a baseline and whether a simpler alternative would work better. Budgets should include training, power, connectivity, security, maintenance and human review, not just the initial purchase. Compare shared or rented computing with new facilities against actual demand and long-term cost.
Public reporting should also show who benefits. A programme concentrated in a handful of well-connected institutions cannot stand in for national progress. Rural communities, smaller businesses, women and persons with disabilities must have a fair opportunity to participate.
Ghana can move faster by learning from tested approaches elsewhere, but leapfrogging cannot mean skipping the foundations on which reliable services depend. The opportunity is to avoid unnecessary mistakes and direct scarce resources towards applications that work.
The country’s success will ultimately be visible in better learning, more productive businesses, stronger farms and safer public systems. It will also be visible in the Ghanaian professionals and enterprises able to build, improve and earn from those services.
Ghana should move with urgency, but measure progress honestly. The prize is an economy better able to solve its own problems and keep more of the rewards. That is the opportunity AI presents, and the standard by which we should judge our response.
